p: So, I just want - thank you and I want to repeat what you said and make sure I heard it right. To build a new school, on average, four years.
Correct.
And what about an extension to any existing schools? The same four years?

Uh, yes, so it takes about a year to design, two to three years to bid out publicly and then uhm and then construction and a lot of our annexes or additions actually are connected to the main building. So there is work to do in the main building as well.

Okay, now you have cited numbers, costs, great. Uhm, a number of seats you’re able to complete within the current envelope of funding. Uhm, the Mayor, the Administration rather has proposed rating the Rainy Day Fund and increasing taxes on middle class New Yorkers and moodies has

shared that you know this could lead to a downgrading of our credit rating. Is that correct?
I have heard that yes.

Okay, how does it impact the work that you are able to do and the funds that you were able to procure in order to build new schools and how it will impact the number of seats that you are able to build?

We cannot not talk to the - speak to the Administration's decision. Uhm, but just a reminder, the funding we use is capital funding. That’s normally obtained by issuing bonds, not necessarily associated with the expense budget.
Right but if borrowing costs increase as a result of lower bond rating, would that impact SCA and your ability to build as many seats? Wouldn’t it increase borrowing costs?
Certainly, additional funding provided will help us with our work to move closer to compliance. As we mentioned before, the $6 billion-

Okay, I’m sorry, I - okay, I know it’s a long day. I either feel like I’m asking it wrong or you’re answering a different

question. If our bond rating is lowered, would that increase costs to borrow money?
I feel like we might need someone from OMB to really speak to that. We’re not bond experts. We just use the funding provided by
Okay.
Sorry about that.

Okay, well I would surmise that if it costs more to borrow money, I would really love SCAs opinion on the exact impact that would have or even a projected impact. I mean these are things that you think about years and years out, right? Like how much - how much money you have, how much cost to borrow, what’s funding the School Construction Authority, and where those dollars go? How many - how much it costs to build seats. Uhm, I’m going to turn it over to Majority Whip Hanks for her questions.

Thank you Chair. Yes, it’s been a long day but uhm, I think we can try to figure out how to answer my questions. So, thank you very much President Kubota and thank you Deputy Chancellor Moran. Uhm, so big thanks to the School Construction Authority for uhm

working - we’ve done some really great projects in the last term and uh, Staten Island Northshore is better for it. Uhm, two years ago, we launched the Northshore Action Plan that promised - that promises thousands of new housing units. Uh, one of the projects that's going to be included is a K-8 school in Stapleton and we have now a recent project to add more school seats for Wall Street in St. George. Uhm, and I believe there could be an opportunity to build another school at the Hungerford site on Thompkins Avenue. Can you expand on how uh, these projects seek to address our boroughs class size compliance?

Sure Council Member, we are very excited about the upcoming projects we have and that includes 25 Wall Street site. We have another site in Epinton. That’s a little bit more south part of this borough and like you mentioned we have the former Hungerford site and that’s ready for us to potentially build a school there. We’re very excited for those projects. A lot of school not currently in compliance and we’re hoping that those projects will provide the much needed support and we would love to

partner with your team, your staff to help us to move those projects, those sites across the finish line. Uhm, so now we can, you know, deliver more seats in a more timely manner.

Thank you and we can definitely talk offline about how the number of those seats are going to be adding to the class size. I think it’s important for all of the Council Members to know like the proposed sites and how they are going to be adding to that, so at least we can answer our constituents but one more question Chair and then I’ll promise I’ll get out of your hair forever. So, as a graduate of La Guardia High School of Music and Performing Arts, I am one of hundreds of children in over the past 30 years. Yes, I say 30 because I graduated in 1990. Uhm, that have a three hour daily commute uh to one of the New York City’s specialized high schools, yet Staten Island is the only borough that does not have a performing arts school. And I really would like to have a commitment from SCA that we will work in earnest to construct one, even some of the ones that are part of those plans that we discussed. Like the former Hungerford

site or uhm, we have to get this done in my last and final term.

Thank you very much, appreciate the question. Kevin Moran. I would say largely the new construction projects are very, very excited on Staten Island with President Kubota’s reference to 25 Wall, which we see as an immediate relief to high schools within that area. I know it’s not designated yet for purpose. It’s being built for high school seats. So, we’re working with Superintendent, CEC, and others to make sure that a sound decision is made to address the very real issue of overcrowded high schools.

Can you just state for the record how many seats that are slated? Because I know we haven’t worked out whether it would be an annex to a local school but you kind of let us know how many seats we’re talking about?

Yeah, it’s about 700. So, it’s a significant relief uh to neighboring high schools. Uhm, I would say also that the St. John Villa development will also relieve some of theirs more immediately school uh - other schools in the district, in your district. I won’t name each

individual school but that would benefit from both 6 to 12 tandems and then a PS school. Uhm, in addition, we did uh previously walk Snug Harbor and SCA did endeavor to do a feasibility study on what a performing arts school could look like. So, we’re certainly active in discussions there and the Hungerford site is something I will absolutely follow up on and see if there’s anything -

Yeah, just so I’m on the record, I’m not married to a location. I think it’s more important to be looking at having a school that satisfies that in the arts in Staten Island but if it - it could be I mean there’s tons of sites that we’re looking at and talking about when it comes to the development under the Northshore Action Plan. We’re slated for over 2,500 units of housing and so, one of the main things that constituents ask for is infrastructure and school seats. So, we just want to make sure that we’re in line. Thank you so much Chair.

Thank you Majority Whip. I got to get that title right, Majority Whip. That’s - that was the acting she learned at La Guardia miming. Uhm, I just want to ask about project

delays. Everyone’s favorite. This has been a concern particularly for members, not just when our local schools are delayed but uhm, coming out of last year's preliminary budget, SCA said they wanted to engage members at an earlier stage in the process of Reso. A project in order to delay - uhm, in order to avoid delays that can pop up later in the process and you know the big joke is like, we fund a project so that our successors can cut the ribbon on it, right? Well, it’s funny to us. How is the project looking in the current fiscal year and has the SCA been able to flag things earlier in the process in order to mitigate delays?

Yes, so thank you for that. So, since our last meeting, uhm, we have piloted a quarterly status report for some Council Members. I think it was received pretty well and we’ve met with most of the new members to introduce ourselves and sort of give general guidance on the Reso. A program because I think some of the issues we were up against also was uh the estimate would be obtained from the school and then it comes to us and then it’s a year later by the way, right? A year later and it’s underfunded and then that sort of starts some of the

delays. And I know that uh, Deputy Chancellor Moran spoke at the expense hearing and it wouldn’t be bad to reiterate some of the reforms we’ve made to sort of the payment process that has actually sped things up on the construction end.

Yeah, absolutely and first and foremost, I’d like to thank you and the Council broadly for their support of schools. I want each Council Member to feel assured that when monies are assigned to a school, that we are responsive and diligent in getting that project done in a reasonable timeframe. So, with that in mind, we sat at the last hearing, uhm, last year with some 700 jobs in our backlog and we took a look at really what were the influencing factors that caused these said delays and to President Kubota’s point, there was a lot that happened. First, was potentially a quote that didn’t line up, increased cost. It could have been a scope change where things significantly changed. So, we set out and put in a few business rules. Number one, we were using a process that didn’t work uh well. Our vendors weren’t being paid. We were advancing capital work with tax levy dollars and

trying to true up at the end of the year. Vendors were not happy with that process. Uh, our teams were not happy and so, what we did with the support of OMB and the SCA was developed a process by which we gathered all our information in one system with a certificate to proceed. A low level work number and we tracked the job with a scope and quote that we had fidelity towards. We didn’t allow the scope to change and say I want to add this one more thing. That would only slow us down, so with that in mind, we started the capital reimbursement process in December and pushed over $210 million, dollar for dollar on capital. It’s one of the best reforms we’ve done in a long, long time in partnership with the SCA and division of school facility. So, the good news here is that I could actually give every Council Member a report now where the projects are. Where they are- for their waiting a purchase order. Whether they’re in scope, design, award and we’re endeavoring to put that on our public website. One of the things we want to make sure is that there’s a level of transparency and accountability that everyone from a parent coordinator, a CEC president, a principal etc., can

all see the project and most notably, the project you award, you can see where it is and I could also text you pictures as the project moves along.

I could say on the record, we get - the football field at JFK, pictures every other week. Uh, now we’re doing the softball field at Walton. All the work looks really beautiful and I know you personally provide those updates but let’s get into just some of the numbers. At last year's hearing, you gave a figure or the SCA gave a figure that 10 percent of member projects in the prior five years had not yet been completed. Has that number been updated to reflect some of the work that uhm, that you shared with us today?

Yeah, in terms of the 700, we’re down to 70 right now. The jobs that were in our backlog, uhm, I can give you actually by year now and categorize them and I can share an actual report with you but we’re down to 70 that are waiting to start from nearly 700.
Yeah, the Committee would like to see - to see that report.

Absolutely and just to give - just to give some color on current jobs, just so you’ll

know what we’re working on. We’re working on 40 bathroom upgrades now, 20 hydroponics labs, 20 gymnasium upgrades, 20 elevator jobs, over a dozen playgrounds, a dozen libraries, 9 cafeterias, 7 stem labs, 6 athletic fields. So, we are keeping busy. Our vendors are in a much better place and the system is working as designed with SCA and our team making sure that work is happening.
And your vendors are being paid on time?
That’s right.
100 percent of them?
That’s right.
Wow. That was - see, that was an easy answer.
It was a very painful year.
Let’s get more answers like that. Yes, 100 percent, yes. Yes or no, yes.

If you spoke to them last year, it was a different story but now we’ve reset and we’ve made sure that no vendor works at risk anymore and that we do have the certificate to proceed, so therefore we can print the purchase order and they could invoice right off that purchase order.
Thank you. I’m turning it over to Council Member Joseph.

Thank you Chair. Thank you so much. Happy to see all of you here. Thank you DC for really stepping up and changing the system and upgrading. Last year was not great at all. So, I would definitely love to see a detailed report on all the projects that I funded in my district. Where they are and uhm I’m still going to ask for PS 217 and the playground. The kids call me all the time. Everytime they call me, I’m calling you. It’s the kids. Uhm, so my question is around uhm, class size. Uhm, last year's hearing, uhm, you testified that 70,000 additional seats would be necessary to meet the class size goals in the law and there are less than half that number in the five year capital plan or only 33,417 seats. Is that still your estimate or has it changed, or is it true that 57 percent of those seats funded have no sites and only 12,426 seats are projected to be completed by September of 2028 deadline for compliance?

Uhm, so it is true that we have uh cited 43 percent of our seats. You know we continue

to cite pretty regularly the exercise that we’ve just gone through with New York City Public Schools has identified a bunch of sites that could be - could receive an addition or annex and we’re going through those one by one before we say it publicly but we - I mean we are 20 months in and you know almost 50 percent cited is pretty good. We have a lot more sites in our pipeline that we’re going through right now and 217 has restarted after the delay because of the weather.

Right, right, right, I know mother nature was not on our side. I know that, so I hope the kids that are listening heard that mother nature was not on our side on that project. Uhm, also uhm, 39 percent of the seats in the plan are unspecific as to district, subdistrict, grade level and when the State Class Law Size uhm, when the State Class Size law and Local Law 167 required New York City Public Schools and SCA to publicly report the details of the needs of the seats by district and grade levels.
We fully believe we’re in compliance with Local Law 167. All the required reports are directly refreshed as new reports become available.
Is it - is it built as you go along, as you see the needs and then you start citing the sites or how does that work?

So, every uhm, Local 167 requires quite a few documents to be published. When we published, when we have updated reports, not just the amendment or you know projection or housing data, uh and bluebook data, we would go back online to post it with the most recent reports.
Do you have a timeline as to when you’ll be posting that?
Uhm, when normally it’s either in the summer for some of the reports and then after November.

Okay, thank you for that. Uhm, is it true that high rises uhm, are going up quickly in many communities and especially in my community where schools are already overcrowded and likely to become more so in the future. Are there proposals to include schools in these plans and I know I did a project like that on uhm, Coney Island for Early Childhood and uhm, it’s also a supermarket desert. One of the things we did with the developer was make sure that there was a supermarket in the

Early Childhood Center because we knew there’s a growing family. Is that one of the things you’re considering as developers are you know building in our communities? Are schools being added to that plan?

Yeah, that’s a great question. Thank you for that. So, yes, if they’re not triggering a school need uh, we work with as many developers as we can for you know sort of a mixed use be at the base of their building. Council Member Restler has introduced us to one in his area. Thank you for that. Uhm, and we you know, we do look to see if we can uhm, have an FAR bump for them as well. So, it makes it beneficial for them as well but yes, we work very well with them.
Wonderful, thank you so much. Chair, I’m done.
Thank you Council Member. Council Member Restler.

Brilliant thank you so much. Uhm, I’d like to firstly, I could use an extra pillow here. Uhm, I always like a little extra height because I need it desperately.

Uhm, i’d like to firstly ask you uh, Deputy Chancellor, President, about something that doesn’t directly, maybe it reports into Kevin. I’m not actually totally sure, is ECF. Uhm, ECF does like one project every five years, which seems like barely a drop in the bucket. We have significant challenges around compliance with the Class Size Law. This is a cost effective way for us to significantly modernize it, improve, expand our school capacity. Why does ECF do such little work?

Well, I think when you look at it, first of all, it’s a great question in the way of thinking that are there opportunities to build classes and class size issues be addressed through uhm, some building developments and private developments and that’s a great question. ECF does do those projects. I think having contractors interested, uhm, is the number one piece and there’s a lot to coordinate. I think if you go to 80 Flatbush, you could see they just recently opened that and two schools at PS and Khalil Gibran and that was a really uhm it’s a really wonderful project. So, looking at how we replicate that and ramp that up

at a speed. We can talk - definitely talk to Jemal who leads that work for us.

Yeah, as you recall Deputy Chancellor, 85 percent in my district. Uhm, PS 287, which is in the beginning stages of a ECF project, it’s in Council Member Hudson’s District but if you walk out on two different sides, you’re in District 33. So, I’m - I’m very familiar with it. And we have a housing crunch where we need to be building a lot more housing. There’s like - everybody is fixated on adding 12 units on top of every library site in the city but we have 1,000- I don’t know - 800,000 school buildings in New York City. Many of which have real potential for development above where we could expand class size, meet - achieve compliance with Class Size Law, build new school facilities. This just feels like a tremendous opportunity that we’re doing almost nothing. Uhm, the projects that are happening, I’m pleased with. I’m supportive of but we should be doing so much more. This just feels like a great opportunity for the Mamdani Administration to really make ACF a relevant agency and have them do real work, rather than one project every five years.

So, appreciate it if you'd look into it and I know that there are folks at City Hall who feel similarly, so I hope we can advance something there together. Uhm, President, I have harangued you in the past about the fact that we put money in for Reso. A projects uhm and it takes six months before they show up in your budget. And so, there’s nothing that you or DCF for that matter can do for over six months after we allocate funds and it’s just dead time. These schools are desperate for the resources that we allocate. If it wasn’t for us, we wouldn’t have new bathrooms, wouldn’t have air conditioning in our gyms and auditoriums. Wouldn’t have all kinds of upgrades for steam and tech and everything in between. How can we fix this? New Administration, fresh set of perspective. How can we make sure that when we’re putting money in for exciting new projects, that we’re not losing six months before we even start?

Yeah, uhm, that is a great question because going over the timeline, right so typically reach out to - or schools reach out to you in the sort of February timeframe. It goes through the City Budget, so July 1, then we- we get the lists. Then

we go to OMB for certificates to proceed. We cannot start work until we receive those CP’s. So, I think we do have an opportunity. Would love to maybe talk to OMB to see how we could streamline that process. So, from the July to December, January, I think we just received some of the CP’s uh just a few weeks ago. So, I mean that’s an entire year.
Seriously.
And I think we can do better. So, happy to talk to our OMB partners.
You think we should give Shareef a really hard time on Wednesday on this topic. Is that what you’re saying? Because I’m happy to do it.
I like Shareef but -

I think that’s not what I thought I heard you testify to but I’m - I’m just kidding. Everybody likes Shareef. Uhm, uh, I want to focus a little bit on Class Size compliance. Uhm, I really appreciate your willingness to try and identify sites for an annex for PSA. That's the number one Class Size challenge for us in District 33 but I’m hearing from a number of my elementary

schools across the district, especially in Greenpoint that they’re really concerned about class size compliance. We know we have a new elementary school coming to the neighborhood. I believe 2029 opening after an extensive 20 plus year engagement process with the community. We are moving forward. Uhm, but I’m very concerned that we don’t even with that new school have the ability to comply with the Class Size Law and meet the demands on Early Childhood Education. And just wondering, with this Administration’s focus on Early Childhood Education, how is that being incorporated into our analysis of capacity in our schools and potentially the need for more school space?

Council Members, we uh explained earlier, capital strategy is only one of the toolkits to help us achieve class size compliance, which is why we have had a really in depth conversation with our partners at uh, New York City Public School to go through district by district, subject by subject, and school by school to really identify, solutions for them. Not every school potentially needs a capital strategy and there might be other non-capital

strategies that might be available. So, exploring all of the pathways to identify the most uhm, efficient ways to help schools achieve near compliance.

Alright, well I just want to say plainly, I think in Greenpoint on the northside, even with the new school coming, I think we have a crunch that I’m concerned about and the other piece - can I do one more question Chair? Do you mind? Thank you. Uhm, I think that I will make this preamble as brief as I can but 20 years ago, the Bloomberg Administration cited a lot of small schools and I don’t feel like anybody in 20 years has really done the analysis. These small schools are doing great and we need to figure out how to ensure that they can serve more kids. I’ll give you an example, the Harry Van Arsdale Campus has three high schools in that building and they’re all great high schools. They’re all bursting at the seams. We don’t have enough space to accommodate any of them and there’s no plan for how we grow them and there’s no plan for how we grow them. You got the A tech campus three blocks away

that’s mostly an empty building, which is not thriving and yet, I haven’t been able to get cooperation from you know folks to say, how do we expand capacity for the high schools that are working where there’s real demand in our community and make that happen. What kind of thinking analysis is going on right now of - these are the small schools that are working that are wanting to serve more kids that would benefit families across our community if they had more capacity. What’s the thinking there?

Well, the commentary there is right on target. Uhm, we’re looking at about 495 schools that have expressed interest in needing more space and they’re kind of like three different buckets if you will. One being potentially like reprogramming the school, minor renovations. The second being some more modest renovations and the third, being potentially an addition and annex or new construction but your first point around how we utilize space is what the Chancellor has charged us recently and we spent a couple three days together uhm, in Long Island City focused as teams with the district planning school construction or facilities and

saying, where do we find places like that? Where can we use proposals to better uhm, match the attributes of the school and the enrollment patterns and then better utilize empty space. So, it is - that is very active on our minds about how we best use it across small schools potentially in large campuses.

And I hope you will consider us as partners because nobody knows the schools in his community better than Eric Dinowitz. I know what’s happening in the schools in my district too. I would be really happy to give you insight into where there’s space, where - who is doing great, where there’s demand. So, I want to just thank, thank you all for the testimony today. Kevin, I think you’ve been testifying for about 15 hours, so good luck with the rest of the afternoon. Thank you all and thank you Chair.

Thank you Council Member and he said he’s committed to staying here till midnight. Did I get that right Kevin? I did want to clarify one thing in your testimony, where you said a 3,066 seat high school in Woodside Queens, that was actually four schools? It’s actually, you were actually building us four

schools. I’ll just share my opinion that once you start breaking up - related to small schools. Once you start breaking up these schools into smaller schools, you really do lose economies of scale and it does make it more challenging to program properly to even out those classes, so that we can have small class sizes without losing a lot of space. So, as you’re - so I would like to see more of the bigger high schools like we used to have in the Bronx, all broken up and there’s not a lot of space uhm or flexibility for everything from AP classes to the space for those R classes to the space for the self contained classes and everything in between. So, you know I want to share that because it is really important to the education that we lose a lot of programming and we lose the ability to program easily, as easily as possible when uhm, when we have such small schools. But I do want to turn it over to Council Member Zhuang for her questions.

Thank you Chair and I am very glad to see Kevin here. Just for the record, we have a date of May 30th in front of PS 97. We want to make sure the AC is going to be installed at that time after two years fighting, more than two years

fighting. Uhm, but I appreciate your work being transparent with us and I have questions for our CEO of the SCA. Uhm, I appreciate Kevin take the shot but in general, in our district schools, even City Council allocated the funding and we don’t see anything built or anything - hear anything back in two years in general. Like I say we give funding for a school to build a new playground, right? Allocate money into South and 24 and we haven’t heard anything back all and it’s very hard to get a response from SCA every time - the answer is always it’s in process. It’s in process. Phase 1, Phase 2, we have no track record. Can you give us a better direction to the public and also parents and the people living in the community, how we check every single project if the City Council Member funded the project.

Yes, thank you for that and yeah, I think it’s - the problem is too full right? We talked about earlier, getting the CP done earlier, so we can actually start the project earlier. So, that’s one side of it. The other side of it is communication with your office, the public and I think Kevin talked about uh trying to pilot getting

like a website for the projects that DSS manages on so that the public can see it. So, we would love to sort of talk to you in your office to see how best you would like that communicated or publicized. Uh, but yes, I agree, we do need to probably engage earlier so that there’s an understanding of where the project is in process. It shouldn’t take two years for you to see any action on - we should be communicating that earlier in the process with you whether it’s under funded, whether there’s a conflict with another project that might be going on that doesn’t allow us to access the playground. Uhm, those things all should be discussed with you and your office.

And the other thing is, I understand SCA wants to get fully funded before to move any project. Uhm, just for the record, the other city agencies, part of their nonprofits, they never get their money funded ahead of time. Like say, a lot of nonprofits, they have to deliver the service first and then they get the reimbursement. I think SCA is very fortunate to get the money before you guys uhm, really actually invest to our community.

The money sitting there for years. We don’t see any progress. If the money was sitting in the bank, probably would get better interest. And we want to see a City Council Member, a mother, my kids go to public school, we like to see the work get done for our kids. Not we invest in a project five years later. We still don’t have a chance to cut to the rebuild or my kids even don’t have a chance to go to the playground that her mother fund- uh, helped to fund the program. So, it’s not fair for all the kids in New York City and also uhm, in the public or public school system, not see any progress about all the projects in the place.
I hear your concerns and I think we - noticed you better this process. So, thank you.
Thank you Council Member. Council Member Wong.
Thank you Chair. Uhm, a very specific question for my district. How many new seats are planned specifically for Council District 30 or School District 24? If you have the data, it would be great.
May we send you the list after this?
Absolutely, absolutely, yeah and do you have any update on IS 93? Because it’s - the construction has been going on - at the 7th year.
Give us one second.
Okay.

Uhm, so just - just for folks that are new to this, so, it was a $19 million masonry roof and parapet window, elevator accessibility project. I know that it did face COVID delays and all of that but and then they - we did have to do some redesign but we will be done by fall.
This year?
This year, yes, 2026.
Thank you. Thank you Chair, thank you.

Thank you. Uhm, last two questions, the SCA had previously testified it would take $4 billion to reach maximum practical accessibility in schools. Meaning the level required to update all schools, it could be physically upgraded without being fully rebuilt. Does SCA have

an updated estimate for how much it would take to get to maximum practical accessibility?
Full accessibility remains a goal of the New York City Public Schools and School COnstruction Authority but that’s married to some logistical obstacles where some older buildings are landlocked and -
Look, I just want to - I agree. We know there are logistical challenges. I just - I’m just asking the $4 billion was testified last year, is that still the same estimate or has that estimate changed?
I don’t think it’s changed much. We’re looking at right now, we have 15 projects that are funded at $204 million for just those 15. So, I think the number is probably going to hold true.
Okay, thank you and lastly, are there any plans for remedial action in the school kitchens that are extremely hot?

Yeah, uh we started uhm, to - we started with one using window AC units where appropriate and where practical to make sure we’re really and focus on ventilation.

The newest work we’re doing now is having split units and we’re working on a project right now with the SCA to do six kitchens with split unit air conditioning and hopefully we can replicate that after we test it and see how it performs but the goal is to bring the temperatures down in the kitchens.
Do you have a survey of how many kitchens are too hot for the workers to you know safely work in the kitchens? And then what the timeline is for the installation of those AC units?

Well, any kitchen that’s too hot, we stop hot meal service and reduce the heat immediately. We don’t use unairconditioned sites in the summer. It’s not an issue right now. Uhm, in terms of uh, this time of year but as the temperatures warm up, we do see it as an issue. So, the survey, I don’t have at my fingertips but I definitely have it. I can get it to you.

Okay, I’m sure you understand. I know you’re working it out but this is a critical issue for you know for the health and safety of our workers and our students. So, we’ll be following up with that as well.
That would be great.

I want to thank you all for your time today, for your testimony. There’s certainly a lot to follow up with regarding the SCA. Uh, but this is you know this is the future of our city. This is the future of our school system and therefore the future of our kids, our kids future. So, thank you for coming in today and we will, I will call the first panel. Okay, I’d like to call up once they clear their things, President of the United Federation of Teachers, Michael Mulgrew. We also have Henry Rubio.
Yes.
Okay, fantastic. Dynamic Duo, let’s - I’ll leave it up to you two to decide who goes first.

He wanted me to go first. Good afternoon, my name is Henry Rubio and I’m humbly serving as the President of the Council for School Supervisors and Administrators and on behalf of nearly 1,800 in service and retired school leaders and Administrators. Thank you Chair for the opportunity to be here with you today. Today, I want to focus on just three matters right now that we think are paramount. Number one,
